clips.text: [warm and conversational] This is OpenCode Junior, our Slack bot. Mention it in a thread, and that thread becomes its own coding agent, with durable state and a real sandboxed computer. Let's follow one message through it.

It starts at the edge. Slack posts the event to a Cloudflare Worker. The Worker verifies the signature, and decodes the envelope. It drops other workspaces, and ambient chatter at the top of a channel. It checks who sent it. Then it writes the event into the thread's mailbox. Only after that write commits does Slack get its two hundred. [confident] That two hundred is a durability receipt. If anything fails first, Slack retries, and the mailbox dedupes by message timestamp.
In the code, it's one short pipeline. A bad signature gets a four oh one. A malformed envelope, a four hundred. Anything not for us is ignored. And the enqueue resolves only after the mailbox write.

Every conversation gets exactly one session object, named by its team, channel, and thread. An alarm wakes it to drain the mailbox, and admission decides what each message means. A mention always wakes the agent. A reply mid-turn steers the running turn. With several people in a thread, a classifier decides, and the rest becomes quiet context. Inside runs an embedded OpenCode runtime, with all its state in the object's own SQLite. Each prompt carries a message ID generated up front, so a retry never submits twice.

The agent's hands live elsewhere. A workspace object owns one Modal sandbox: a real virtual machine running a small daemon. Shell commands and file edits cross into it; text-only replies don't wait for it. Every hour, a template registry prepares a checkout of the OpenCode repo with its dependencies installed, so cloning it is a mount, not a download. After twenty idle minutes, the sandbox is snapshotted and shut down, and restored the next time it's needed.

Now the answer travels back. A follower reads OpenCode's durable event log and folds it into a turn. Each assistant message becomes one Slack post, edited in place as it streams, with a working indicator above it, and a footer only for substantial or failed turns. Slack has no idempotency key for new posts. So before posting, Junior flushes a write-ahead intent, and stamps the post's identity into Slack metadata. After a crash, it finds that post and adopts it, instead of posting twice.

One rule shapes all of this. When a durable object resets, its unflushed writes roll back, but Slack posts it already sent still stand. So every coordinator pass is time-boxed, and returns before the platform's limit. Writes that must survive are flushed before the side effect. Alarms are backstops, not poll loops. And storage is never migrated: a schema version mismatch wipes the tables and starts fresh.

A few shared objects sit around this core. Some tools, like a GitHub comment, need a human's approval. The call is recorded with its full arguments, a card is posted, and the turn ends. When someone clicks approve, pending to executing commits first, so a double click never runs it twice. Then the result wakes the model. Each team has a scheduler object: a schedule fires as an ordinary new session, and after downtime it fires once, late, never in a burst. Behind the web dashboard, settings and connectors objects hold configuration and connections.
[warm] That's the shape. Slack hits the edge. Each thread gets one durable object. The work happens in a sandbox, and the answer flows back into Slack. Next time, we'll look at where it's heading.
